working_title: Scotland's Northern Isles: A Practical Guide to Playing Golf in Orkney and Shetland
angle: Orkney and Shetland are routinely overlooked by travelling golfers who head straight for the Highlands or the Hebrides, yet they offer some of the most characterful, affordable, and logistically interesting golf in Britain. The post frames the trip as a genuine adventure rather than a pilgrimage to a famous name, covering the key courses on both island groups and the practicalities of actually getting there and getting around.
research_notes:
- Orkney has two mainland courses (Orkney Golf Club in Kirkwall, Stromness Golf Club) and two island courses (South Ronaldsay Golf Club in St Margaret's Hope, Westray Golf Club on Westray). Orkney Golf Club was founded in 1889 and is the oldest and longest in Orkney; it hosted the golf competition for the 2025 Island Games.
- Stromness Golf Club is described as one of the most picturesque courses in the UK; many holes have views over Hoy Sound and the Hoy Hills, with the course just over 4,800 yards — short but testing in the wind.
- South Ronaldsay Golf Club opened in 2005; nine holes with eighteen tees available, described as possibly the most challenging in Orkney. Reached by driving across all four Churchill Barriers from Kirkwall.
- Westray Golf Club: nine holes on the island of Westray (a short flight or ferry from Kirkwall). Its third hole measures 738 yards and is claimed to be the longest hole in British golf. No booking required; honesty-box green fee. Located next to Noltland Castle, walking distance from Pierowall village.
- Orkney Golf Club is a non-profit run by volunteers; honesty-box payment in use at some courses. Green fees across the Northern Isles described as 'remarkably cheap' compared to the rest of Scotland.
- In midsummer, 'Open Midnight Golf' is a feature on the Orkney Golf Club fixture card.
- Shetland has two 18-hole courses and three smaller courses. Shetland Golf Club at Dale (just north of Lerwick) is the main 18-hole track; parkland, over 5,500 yards, hilly, windy, club hire available (cash/cheque only).
- Whalsay Golf Club on the island of Whalsay (30-minute ferry from Shetland Mainland) is described as one of the highest-rated visitor courses anywhere in the UK; Britain's most northerly golf course. Panoramic views; wildlife interruptions (gulls, skuas, seals, porpoises) and occasional charter planes landing at the adjacent airstrip.
- Asta Golf Course: nine holes near Scalloway/Tingwall, good for visitors who want a gentler test.
- The Knab: public nine-hole course in Lerwick town centre, walkable from the historic centre.
- Fair Isle: remote six-hole 'Lighthouse Keeper's Golf Course', established in the early 20th century; accessible by ferry or small plane from Shetland Mainland. Also a whale-watching spot.
- Shetland offers the possibility of 'simmer dim' (midnight sun) golf in summer months.
- Practical travel: NorthLink Ferries serve both Orkney (Aberdeen/Scrabster to Stromness/Kirkwall) and Shetland (Aberdeen to Lerwick). Loganair operates flights to Kirkwall and Lerwick from several Scottish airports. Inter-island travel on Orkney and Shetland uses small ferries and Loganair inter-island flights.
- Clubhouses on these islands are often volunteer-run and not always staffed; visitors should plan ahead and not rely on facilities being open on arrival.
- Wildlife on courses includes nesting birds, Orkney voles, rabbits (Orkney Golf Club notes no dog walking allowed for this reason).
